title: Contentment is wealth (201–204)
hookLine: victory breeds hatred; health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204)

lines: THE RAISE FEELS GREAT FOR TWO WEEKS.
YOU WIN, AND THE ROOM FEELS WORSE.
A FINISH LINE THAT KEEPS MOVING.
cards: You get the raise. For about two weeks it feels wonderful. Then the new number becomes the normal number, and you start noticing what the next one would buy.
Or you win the argument, the other person goes quiet, and somehow the room feels worse than before. It's a finish line that keeps moving.
There's a word for being able to stop at the line you're already standing on, and today's verse calls it the best kind of money there is.

teach.b: Verse two oh one, in Max Müller's words: "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy."
The commentary says the Buddha spoke it after King Pasenadi of Kosala lost a battle to his own nephew and couldn't eat or sleep for shame. Winning makes an enemy; losing makes you miserable.
The only way out of that seesaw is to step off it.
Then the chapter's great list, verse two oh four: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness."
The Pali for contentment is santuṭṭhi, being satisfied with what's there. It isn't laziness, or giving up on improving things. It's the ability to stop feeling poor when you have enough.
There's a lovely story behind that verse too.

teach.h: A KING WHO ATE TOO MUCH.
teach.b: The same King Pasenadi, the commentary says, ate so much at every meal that he could barely stay awake to hear the Buddha teach. The Buddha suggested he eat a little less, mindfully.
The king had his nephew recite a short verse at every meal as a reminder, cut back bit by bit, grew slim and well, and came back to thank him.
Health, the greatest gift. And notice where the list ends: trust as the best kinship, and nibbāna, the deepest ease, as the highest happiness. None of the four is for sale.

how: Contentment with little is one of the qualities Buddhist monastics are trained in, and lay Buddhists often quote verse 204 as everyday wisdom about health, enough and trust.

o: being satisfied with what you already have
giving up on trying to improve anything
the riches a king wins by victory in battle

s: contentment in this verse means never trying to improve anything
santuṭṭhi is being satisfied with enough, not giving up.
in the commentary, King Pasenadi learned to eat less and grew well
his nephew recited a verse at each meal as a reminder.

games.q: you're King Pasenadi. you've just lost a battle to your own nephew. you can't eat or sleep. what does verse 201 suggest?
o: raise a bigger army and win next time.
give up both victory and defeat, and be content.
games.why: winning makes an enemy; losing makes you miserable. "he, the contented, is happy."

practice: Name, slowly, three things in your life that are already enough, not perfect, just enough: maybe the bed you slept in, a pair of shoes that fit, one person who would pick up if you called.
As you name each one, breathe out a little longer, the way you'd sigh after a good meal. If a voice says yes, but, let it talk without following it, and stay with your three enoughs.

wordCard.voice: Santuṭṭhi. Contentment, being satisfied with what's there: verse two oh four says health is the greatest gift, contentment the best riches, trust the best kinship, nibbāna the highest happiness.

orig.note: Pali: contentment, being satisfied with what's there — santuṭṭhi-paramaṃ dhanaṃ, contentment the best wealth.

carryVoice: Your line: health is the greatest gift. Contentment, the best riches. Day one hundred ninety-seven, done.
